question: What stays recognisable when a dance fills with faster notes?
intro: A gavotte becomes six variations, each retaining its harmonic route while changing the keyboard writing. Marcelle Meyer plays this harpsichord work on piano: follow the points of rest through the increasingly busy surface.

relations.label: The gavotte’s second strain repeats
relations.basis: The gavotte has two repeated strains, the second twice the length of the first. These excerpts lie in that longer strain and its repeat before the first double. CENS diagonal mean 0.957, sustained 25 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 27 s (cache/form/rameau-gavotte-six-doubles.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The first double repeats its second strain
relations.basis: The first double retains the gavotte’s repeated-strain design while adding upper figuration. These excerpts compare the same strain within that double. CENS diagonal mean 0.975, sustained 16.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 19 s (cache/form/rameau-gavotte-six-doubles.txt, candidate 3; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The harmonic route survives another double
relations.basis: The fifth and sixth doubles preserve the gavotte’s harmonic route while changing the keyboard figuration. The long paired excerpts lie in their later strains; the relation does not claim identical melody or finger-work. CENS diagonal mean 0.929, sustained 26.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 50 s (cache/form/rameau-gavotte-six-doubles.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Remember the points of rest
cues.text: The gavotte sets out two repeated strains before the six doubles, or variations. Remember where each phrase comes to rest as well as the tune itself: those resting places help connect the later, faster-moving writing to its model.
cues.evidence: Nicolas Martello’s score discussion identifies the repeated two-part theme and the six variations. This cue describes that design rather than assigning individual cadences to seconds: https://www.edmu.fr/p/rameau.html
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Before the Paris operas
cues.text: Rameau worked as an organist in several French cities, including Clermont, before settling in Paris in the early 1720s. His career as a church musician preceded his success at the Paris Opéra.
cues.evidence: M. Elizabeth C. Bartlet traces Rameau’s organist posts and move to Paris in her biographical article: https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/literature-and-arts/music-history-composers-and-performers-biographies/jean-philippe-rameau-0

cues.title: More notes, the same route
cues.text: The opening variations fill the theme’s spaces with quicker notes. Listen for a slower line beneath the activity: variation changes the way the harmony is presented without discarding the dance’s basic route.
cues.evidence: The score discussion describes faster notes added around the theme in the first doubles. A sustained rise in detected attacks after about 1:25 supports this provisional location: https://www.edmu.fr/p/rameau.html
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A theory of chord roots
cues.text: Rameau published his Traité de l’harmonie in 1722. His fundamental bass follows the roots of chords, not necessarily their lowest sounding notes: different arrangements of one chord can therefore share a harmonic identity.
cues.evidence: Bartlet’s article dates the treatise and explains Rameau’s account of chord roots and inversions: https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/literature-and-arts/music-history-composers-and-performers-biographies/jean-philippe-rameau-0

cues.title: The moving line changes place
cues.text: Across the first two doubles, the quicker writing passes between the upper and lower parts. Try listening beneath the tune rather than always following the highest notes. The most active part need not be the melody.
cues.evidence: The score discussion describes the exchange of roles between the first and second doubles. Their placement in this recording is estimated from the variation order and changes in activity, not aligned note by note: https://www.edmu.fr/p/rameau.html
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Listen between the outer parts
cues.text: A keyboard texture can contain more than a tune and a bass. In these variations, listen for a moving line between the highest and lowest notes, and notice whether the outer parts seem to hold it in place.
cues.evidence: The score discussion describes inner-part movement in the third double. The change in activity around 3:15 is a provisional guide to the surrounding variation, not proof of an exact boundary: https://www.edmu.fr/p/rameau.html
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A stage debut at fifty
cues.text: Hippolyte et Aricie reached the Paris Opéra in 1733, when Rameau was fifty. His theoretical writings and keyboard publications were already in circulation before this new phase of his career.
cues.evidence: Bartlet dates the Opéra debut to 1733 and places the treatise and harpsichord books before it: https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/literature-and-arts/music-history-composers-and-performers-biographies/jean-philippe-rameau-0

cues.title: Repetition as movement
cues.text: Repeated notes can make a passage feel busy even when the pitch stays still. Listen for the distinction between a succession of fresh attacks and a melody that travels up or down.
cues.evidence: Repeated-note writing is a feature of the fourth double in the score discussion. The recording’s dense attack pattern across roughly 4:10–4:45 supports a broad passage cue, not an exact score alignment: https://www.edmu.fr/p/rameau.html
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The longer shape inside the activity
cues.text: Try following the phrase across the rapid notes rather than hearing each attack as a separate event. Where does the harmony seem to be going, and which familiar point of rest tells you it has arrived?
cues.evidence: This is a listening prompt about the shared harmonic design of the doubles. It does not claim a particular note or hand movement at this time.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The final variation still belongs to the dance
cues.text: Compare this late, active writing with the plain gavotte. Can you recognise the phrase lengths and resting points even when the surface no longer resembles the opening melody closely?
cues.evidence: The sixth double closes the score’s variation sequence. Its approximate location follows the order and proportions of the preceding doubles; no bar-level timing has been verified: https://www.edmu.fr/p/rameau.html
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Let the last phrase finish
cues.text: Follow the final phrase from its active notes into the remaining resonance. The ending belongs to the last variation rather than a separate restatement of the original gavotte.
cues.evidence: The feature report shows a marked reduction in attacks and recorded level across the closing seconds. The score discussion places no return of the plain theme after the sixth double: https://www.edmu.fr/p/rameau.html

transitions.title: The dance acquires a running upper part
transitions.how: The gavotte completes its cadence on A before the first double restarts the same harmonic route. Rameau changes the mechanism of motion: the ornamented dance tune becomes a slower, chordal line in the left hand, while continuous semiquavers run above it in the right. The two-beat metre stays intact; the new surface is not a newly notated metre or an intervening modulation. On Meyer’s piano, listen through the extra resonance for the moment the upper part stops punctuating the dance and starts filling its spaces.
transitions.evidence: The first double is provisionally mapped at 84 s. The theme’s repeated strain is matched through 81 s, and the analysis shows sustained higher attack density from 1:25. Martello’s score discussion identifies the left-hand chorale-like theme and continuous right-hand semiquavers: https://www.edmu.fr/p/rameau.html . No attacca marking or score-mandated acceleration is claimed.

transitions.title: Flowing counterpoint becomes repeated attack
transitions.how: The third double’s interlocking voices close their A-centred circuit before the fourth resets the texture around equal repeated notes. Rameau preserves the gavotte’s harmonic and phrase plan but changes what the hands must do: rapid rearticulation replaces the preceding flowing counterpoint. Repetition can therefore increase the sense of activity without sending the melody through more pitches. Meyer’s piano makes each fresh attack and its decay audible; the join depends on that new articulation, not on a change of key or metre.
transitions.evidence: The fourth double starts at the map’s 248 s boundary, also the report’s 4:08 change. Dense attacks follow across 4:10–4:45. Martello distinguishes the third double’s four-part counterpoint from the fourth’s equal repeated notes: https://www.edmu.fr/p/rameau.html . Other routine variation resets are omitted; there is no final return of the plain theme.

composer.epithet: A theorist of chord roots who began his operatic career at fifty and made harmonic surprise part of French theatrical action.
facts: Organist in French provincial cities, including Clermont-Ferrand; first harpsichord book published in 1706
Traité de l’harmonie, 1722; Nouveau système de musique théorique, 1726
First opera, Hippolyte et Aricie, 1733; tragédies en musique, opéras-ballets and court entertainments
composer.background:
Rameau was born in Dijon, where his father worked as an organist. The documentation of his first four decades is much thinner than that of his Parisian operatic career. He held church appointments in several French cities, published a first book of harpsichord pieces in Paris in 1706, and worked again at Clermont-Ferrand before settling permanently in the capital in the early 1720s. Keyboards, church duties and the analysis of musical practice formed his training. By the time he wrote his first surviving opera he had already published the theoretical book for which his name was known.

The Traité de l’harmonie réduite à ses principes naturels appeared in 1722. Rameau proposed that chords and their connections could be understood through a fundamental bass. Inversion became central: a chord could retain its identity while one of its upper notes moved into the bass. His explanations developed across later books, and his claims to a foundation in nature changed as he engaged with acoustics. The theory attempts to explain why harmonic progressions cohere.
